title: Aperture
question: Why do camera numbers go 8, 11, 16?
hook: Every proper camera carries the same strange row: 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16. It looks random. It isn't. Each number lets in half the light of the one before, and the reason is a shape you met at primary school: the circle. Your camera has three of them, on a yellow wheel.

sections.title: Your guess first
sections.q: Which lets in more light, f/8 or f/16? And how much more?
choices: f/16, twice as much: 16 is twice 8
sections.reveal: Most people say f/16, twice, because sixteen is twice eight. It's the other way round, and it's more than twice. An f/16 hole is half as wide as an f/8 hole. And half as wide doesn't let in half the light. It lets in a quarter. Here's why.

sections.title: Width is not the point. Area is.
sections.body:
Behind the lens sits a hole that decides how much light gets through: the aperture. Your camera calls its three holes dots.

Light comes through the whole of a hole, so what counts is its area, and area grows with width times width. Twice as wide lets in four times the light.

Photographers name a hole by how many times it fits into the lens's length: the f-number. Your lens is 32 mm, so a 2 mm hole is 32 ÷ 2 = f/16. Bigger number, smaller hole. And since the same f-number gives the same brightness on any lens, long or short, it became the universal language of light.

To double the light the area must double, so the width grows by √2, about 1.41. Divide by 1.41 again and again: 16, 11.3, 8, 5.7, 4. Round them, and there is the row.

figure.caption: Twice the width, four times the area.

timeline.what: Sutton and Dawson describe a hole as a share of the lens's length: the f-number idea.
Hurter and Driffield measure how plates darken with light, and give plates speed numbers.
The American ASA film speed scale: double the number, half the light.
International standards bring the American and German scales together. Hence 'ISO 400' on the box.

sections.title: Slide the dot, build the row

sims.intro: Your camera's three holes on squared paper. Slide the width, count squares, watch the light on the film.
sims.after: Small to middle is about double (× 2.16): one step. Middle to large adds about a third. The picture never got bigger, only brighter: the lens makes the picture, the hole decides how much light makes it.

sims.intro: Find the step that makes each hole let in exactly twice the light of the one before.
sims.after: Divide by 1.41 each time and every step doubles the light; every second step doubles the width. That's the row printed on cameras for a hundred years.

sections.title: The wheel and its three dots
sections.alt: The inside of the orange front plate, with the yellow wheel and its three holes
sections.caption: Inside the front plate: the wheel with three holes.
sections.body:
The wheel sits behind the lens inside the front plate. A handle on the front turns it and a springy tooth clicks into one of three notches, so a hole always stops exactly behind the lens. Small 1.96 mm (f/16), middle 2.88 mm (f/11), large 3.34 mm (f/9.5).

Which dot, with ISO 400 film: full sun, small; hazy sun, middle; bright cloud, large. Darker than that, hold the rocker open and count. The large dot stops at f/9.5, not f/8, because a single lens gets soft away from the middle when the hole grows. That's the trade.

sections.title: One hole, wide open
sections.body: Most phones have a single hole that never changes, usually wider than f/2, about as wide across as your large dot but in front of a lens only a few millimetres long. A few models have had two settings. So a phone can't pick a dot. It controls light with the other two settings instead: how long it collects, and how much it amplifies. That's lesson 9.

sections.title: Your three dots, in steps of light
sections.summary: one sum, with the real numbers
lines: light goes with area: width × width
sections.body: The model's own table says f/16.4 for the small dot: a printed hole comes out a touch smaller than drawn.

sections.title: Three dots on tracing paper
needs: your camera, with no film inside
a strip of tracing paper, about 4 cm wide
a room with one bright window
steps: Take the back off. Tape the tracing paper over the two curved rails, where the film would lie.
Set the small dot. Press the rocker to its middle click and hold it: the shutter stays open.
Point the camera at the window and look at the tracing paper from behind.
Still holding the rocker, slide to the middle dot, then the large.
On squared paper draw circles 19.6, 28.8 and 33.4 mm across (ten times the holes). Count the squares in each.
sections.notice: The window gets brighter, never bigger. And the squares come out close to 1 : 2.2 : 2.9.

items.why: The f-number is the lens's length divided by the hole's width. A bigger number means a smaller hole.

items.q: A hole twice as wide lets in…
items.why: Twice as wide and twice as tall: four times the area, four times the light.

items.q: Why is the row 8, 11, 16 and not 8, 12, 16?
choices: Each step doubles the light, which needs 1.41 times the width
items.why: Doubling the area takes √2 ≈ 1.41 times the width: 8 × 1.41 = 11.3, rounded to 11; 11.3 × 1.41 = 16.

items.q: Middle dot 2.88 mm, large dot 3.34 mm. How much more light does the large one give?
items.why: 3.34 ÷ 2.88 = 1.16, and light goes with the square: 1.16 × 1.16 = 1.35.

items.q: Why does the large dot stop at f/9.5 and not go to f/8?
choices: f/8 would let in less light
A bigger hole makes a single lens softer away from the middle
f/8 is not a real setting
items.why: f/8 would need a 4.0 mm hole (32 ÷ 8): about half a step more light than the large dot, but a single lens gets softer away from the middle as the hole grows. So the wheel stops at 3.34 mm.

sections.title: Try it on your roll
sections.lead: One scene, three dots. The cheapest experiment in photography.
shots: Find a scene in hazy sun, with soft shadows. Small dot, one press.
Same spot, same scene: middle dot.
Same again: large dot. Write down which frame was which.
sections.look: Hazy sun is the middle dot's light, so the middle frame should look right, the small one a little darker, the large one a little lighter. Small to middle doubles the light; middle to large adds only a third, so the last two look closer than the first two.

sections.body: The hole decides how bright. Something else decides how long.

units.title: Check yourself
units.what: 5 questions, then 3 pictures to take on your roll in your own time.

objectives: Say why a bigger f-number is a smaller hole (it is the lens's length divided by the hole's width).
Show that twice the width is four times the area, and so four times the light.
Explain why each step in the row 8, 11, 16 is 1.41 times the one before, and that each step doubles or halves the light.
Use this camera's three widths to show that small to middle doubles the light and middle to large adds about a third.
Choose a dot for the light outside, and say why the large dot is not bigger.
materials: per group of three: a built camera with no film inside, a strip of tracing paper, tape
squared paper (5 mm), a compass or round things to draw round, a calculator
a room with one window as the only light
teach.exit_ticket: In one sentence: why is f/16 a smaller hole than f/8? And one number: how many times more light does a hole twice as wide let in?
teach.misconception: That a bigger f-number means a bigger hole, and that light goes up in step with the width. The f-number is length ÷ width; light goes with the area, width × width; one step on the row is 1.41 times the width and twice the light.

differentiation.support: Use squares only, not circles: 1, 2 and 3 squares wide, and count. Give the ladder sim's three buttons instead of the slider. For the sum, give the divisions and ask only for the squaring.
differentiation.stretch: Work out the area of each dot with π r² and compare with the square counts. Then: a camera has shutter speeds 1/250 and 1/500. Which f-number at 1/500 gives the same picture as f/11 at 1/250? (f/8.)
differentiation.access: Each sim has a text line saying what it shows. The squared-paper task can use printed circles of the right sizes for students who find drawing them hard.

teach.safety: Nobody points the camera, or looks, at the sun. No film in the camera during the tracing-paper activity.

period.what: The question; hold up the yellow wheel. Everyone answers the f/8 or f/16 question on paper; count the votes.
'Width is not the point. Area is.' on the board: a square and one twice as wide; then two circles on squared paper.
Squared-paper circles in threes: 2, 3, 4 and 5.6 cm across. Count the squares, divide each by the one before. Which pair doubles?
The ladder sim, whole class: who finds × 2.00 first? Then the sum on the board with the camera's three dots.
The Try card: tracing paper behind the open camera, the three dots in turn. Finished groups choose a dot for today's sky with the chart.
Exit ticket; return to the opening vote.

questions.q: Which is the bigger hole, f/8 or f/16?
questions.a: f/8. The f-number is the lens's length divided by the hole's width: a bigger number is a smaller hole.

questions.q: A hole twice as wide lets in how much more light?
questions.a: Four times: twice as wide and twice as tall.

questions.q: Why is the row 8, 11, 16 and not 8, 12, 16?
questions.a: Each step doubles the light, which takes √2 ≈ 1.41 times the width: 8 × 1.41 ≈ 11, 11 × 1.41 ≈ 16.

questions.q: Small dot 1.96 mm, middle 2.88 mm. How much more light?
Full sun, ISO 400 film. Which dot, and which old rule does that match?
questions.a: The small dot, f/16: the sunny-16 rule, f/16 at about 1 ÷ ISO of a second.
